newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Crude Outlook - refinery demand to fall short.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Crude Outlook - refinery demand to fall short.

text.p: Expected increases in U.S. refinery production will fail to alter market dynamics to any great extent this week, leaving domestic markets flush with an abundance of crude oil, traders and analysts said Monday.
This week's outlook for the crude market called for a weakening trend as supportive news from a variety of world hotspots was already accounted for in prices.
Left to fundamentals alone, crude prices should test lower ranges, under $20.00 per barrel for spot June West Texas Intermediate/Cushing.

"The scope of the increase should push refinery runs up 200,000 barrels per day in the next two to three weeks, but we shouldn't see any material impact on prices," said William Brown, president of W.H. Brown & Co in New York.
Non-OPEC production increases have been sufficient to keep markets well-supplied, traders noted.

Brown said a peak in crude prices usually comes in May, following gasoline price gains during the traditional gasoline "driving" season in the run-up to the Memorial Day holiday at the end of the month.

But this year the heating oil market has stolen the thunder and gasoline's rally has been non-existent. From the start of February to the end of April last year gasoline futures soared from just above 52 cents to 77 cents a gallon, but during the same period this year they've have fallen from around 68 cents to just above 62 cents.
"It doesn't seem to be happening, with imports remaining high and more than adequate second-quarter crude avails (availabilities)," said Brown.
While outright crude prices lurch lower, cash traders expected June domestic grades to hover at unchanged to slightly firmer differentials.
Monday marked the first day of trading for June as the prompt-month in the physical market, leaving the market dulled on the typical changeover hangover.

"It's not going to get real active in here until at least the first of the month (May)," said one Texas broker, though he noted that June barrels were coming in below the prices which had prevailed for May.

June Light Louisiana Sweet/St. James was pegged at steady to 10 cents under WTI/Cushing. Absorption of North Sea Brent barrels by thirsty refiners in the previous two weeks had supported an LLS rally from discounts of more than 40 cts to the WTI, to slightly positive May numbers last week.
But traders do not think the trend will continue.
"There will be a pick-up in North Sea supply coming to the U.S. Gulf, even if prices have firmed there in the last week or so," said a foreign crude trader in the U.S. Gulf.
Sour grades returned to bearish numbers for June, with West Texas Sour and Eugene Island barrels both talked at more than $1.65-75 under the WTI/Cushing marker.
Traders said Middle East and Nigerian tensions would be key outside news influences on the market this week.
"There seems to be about nine different political stories that could each pop the market up $4 (a barrel) if they explode," said a cash dealer.
Iraq's sanctions-busting pilgrim air flights to Mecca came and went in the last two weeks without any military action, though they underlined the potential for heightened tension there.

In Nigeria, tribal fighting in the oil-producing Warri region forced Shell to cut production 20 percent at Forcados late last week. Though cargoes will only be delayed, the move helped to keep LLS prices firm as the Louisiana grade moves in competition with sweet West African barrels.
--Patrick Connole, New York Energy Desk, +1 212 859 1828
